{{Short description|Estonian-born atomic physicist}}{{EngvarB|date=June 2025}}
	
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2025}}

'''Uuno Öpik''' (a.k.a. Uno Öpik; 19 October 1926 in [[Tartu|Tartu, Estonia]] – 30 April 2005 in [[Bath, Somerset|Bath, UK]]) was an Estonian-born [[Atomic physics|atomic physicist]] most of whose adult life was spent in [[Northern Ireland]] and Great Britain.<ref name=epersons/>

==Pseudo Jahn–Teller effect==
In the 1957 paper "Studies of the Jahn-Teller effect. I. A survey of the static problem",<ref name=JahnTeller/> the authors (Uuno Öpik & Maurice Henry Lecorney Pryce) formulated the [[Pseudo Jahn–Teller effect]] (PJTE) problem for the first time, and demonstrated that this mechanism is a source of instability in polyatomic systems (molecules and solids). This is discussed in [Bersuker],<ref name=bersuker/> which credits [Opik & Pryce] as an early treatment of vibronic instability in molecular and solid-state systems.<ref name=volokov/>

==Life and career==
Uuno Öpik graduated from Tartu 1st Gymnasium in 1943.<ref name=ulster/> In 1943 his father Ernst moved the family to [[Gdańsk|Danzig]], and then to [[Swinemünde]] and finally to [[Hamburg]]. From 1946 to 1948 he studied at the [[Baltic University]].<ref name=ulster/> In 1948 the family moved to [[Northern Ireland]], when his father joined the staff at the [[Armagh Observatory]].<ref name=tartu/> In 1950 he became a member of [[Student Society Liivika]].<ref name=keskus/>

Öpik studied at [[Queen's University Belfast]] (QUB), getting a BSc in mathematics in 1950, a BSc in physics in 1951, and a PhD in physics in 1954  with the thesis, "Quantal investigations of certain excitation and ionization processes" under the advisor [[David Bates (physicist)|David Bates]].<ref name=mgp/>

He worked as a research fellow at the [[University of Bristol]] from 1955 to 1956, as a lecturer at the [[Aberystwyth University|University of Aberystwyth]] in Wales from 1956 to 1986 and at the [[University of Reading]] from 1960 to 1962.  In 1962, he returned to QUB, where he served on the staff until retirement in 1986.<ref name=epersons/>  His doctoral students included [[Raymond Flannery]] and Hugh Morrison.<ref name=mgp/>

He was one of six children of Estonian [[astronomer]] and [[astrophysicist]] [[Ernst Öpik]].<ref name=keskus/> His son is the British politician [[Lembit Öpik]].<ref name=ulster/>
